entry.title: Glossary
entry.summary: Short definitions of the acronyms used across the pages (GPU, MPI, NUMA, RDMA, QoS and more), each with a pointer to the page that explains it properly.

entry.title: The Morning After the Upgrade: Smoke Tests for the Change You Cannot Undo
entry.summary: What to check around a Slurm upgrade: a backup proven by restoring it, versions on every node, a before/after snapshot, the control-plane smoke test, and why downgrading is not supported.

entry.title: Measure Twice, Reconfigure Once: Smoke-Testing a slurm.conf Change
entry.summary: What a bad slurm.conf does (typo, partition naming a missing node) and the dry runs that catch it first: a snapshot diff, sbatch --test-only and a canary partition.

entry.title: The Cluster That Worked Perfectly and Remembered Nothing: a Two-Minute Slurm Smoke Test
entry.summary: A six-check, two-minute Slurm smoke test (MUNGE, controller, nodes, srun, sbatch, sacct) as one script with three outcomes, tested against four injected failures and a busy cluster.

entry.title: Back From the Repair Shop: Is This Node Fit to Return to Service?
entry.summary: Why idle does not mean a node is healthy, what Slurm does when hardware and slurm.conf disagree (and how configoverrides hides it), and a reservation fence for a probe job.

entry.title: Does the Rulebook Still Work? Smoke-Testing QOS, Submit Rules and Preemption
entry.summary: A two-stage smoke test for QOS, submit rules and preemption: routing and refusals with no resources, then a real eviction and requeue, with a full script and its output.

entry.title: When Smoke Becomes a Fire Drill: SchedMD's Test Suite, ReFrame and the Baseline Rule
entry.summary: What SchedMD's test suite and ReFrame do, how both were run against a live test cluster, and why results only mean something against a baseline taken before the change.

entry.title: Autopsy of a Job: Reading sacct Like a Coroner
entry.summary: How to find out what happened to a job that has gone, with sacct states, exit codes (exit:signal), requeued runs, useful fields, and the neighbors scontrol, sstat and sreport.

entry.title: Coins and Calls: Binomial and Poisson as Recipes
entry.summary: A named distribution is a recipe for who gets how much probability. Binomial fits "how many yeses in n tries", Poisson fits "how many events in a window". Know the question and the assumptions.

entry.title: Counting the Ways: Probability as a Share of the List
entry.summary: Probability is the share of the equally likely ways. So "or" adds, "and" multiplies, and "at least one" is 1 minus none, because of what each does to the list of ways.

entry.title: How Sure Are You? Confidence Intervals
entry.summary: A confidence interval is an honest "about this, give or take": the estimate plus or minus a margin built from the standard error. The 95% describes the method, not one interval.

entry.title: The Bell Curve: Probability as Area, and One Ruler for Every Bell
entry.summary: Many small nudges add up to a bell. For continuous data probability is area, and the z-score makes every bell the same bell, so one table serves all of them, until the data are not a bell.

entry.title: The Courtroom for Numbers: Could Plain Luck Do This?
entry.summary: A hypothesis test asks one question: could plain luck have produced a difference this big? Shuffle the labels and count. What the p-value is, what it is not, and how testing twenty things fools you.

entry.title: The Test That Was 99% Accurate: Conditional Probability and Bayes' Rule
entry.summary: Conditional probability is "shrink the crowd to those who match, then count again". Bayes' rule is that count read the other way; a tree of whole tins shows why a 99% test is often wrong.

entry.title: Two Things Moving Together: Correlation and the Line
entry.summary: Correlation is the average product of paired z-scores, a number about straight-line togetherness only. The regression line is least squared walking applied to a line. Graph first, always.

entry.title: What to Expect: Random Variables and Expected Value
entry.summary: A random variable is a number attached to each way things could turn out. Expected value and variance are the mean and the leftover walk of earlier parts, weighted by probability instead of frequency.

entry.title: Why Averages Behave: The Sip You Could Take a Thousand Times
entry.summary: An average is itself random: every sample gives a different one. Their spread shrinks as sigma over root n, and whatever the crowd looks like, sample averages pile into a bell. Bias is not cured.

entry.title: How Far From the Middle? One Question Behind Every Summary Number
entry.summary: Mean, median and mode are one question asked with three rulers: how much should a long walk hurt? Spread is what is left over. Variance, SD, IQR and the n-1 mystery fall out of that.

entry.title: The Map of Leaf & Kettle: Every Idea So Far in One Walk Through the Shop
entry.summary: A concept map, decision chart and definitions sheet for the whole series, as a memory palace in one tea shop: nine rooms for describing data, an upstairs for chance.

entry.title: Where Do You Stand? Percentiles, Z-Scores and the Box Plot
entry.summary: A score means nothing without its crowd. Two rulers give it a position: rank (percentile) and distance in spreads (z-score). The box plot is just the ogive read at four landmarks.

entry.title: Mira's Notebook: What Kind of Data Is This, and How Do You Count It?
entry.summary: Why you cannot average a blend name: the four kinds of data, and how to turn raw numbers into honest category, ungrouped and grouped frequency tables.

entry.title: Draw It Before You Describe It: Three Pictures of the Same Fifty Days
entry.summary: Why a table of counts glazes eyes and a picture does not: the histogram, frequency polygon and ogive built from one table, and the mistakes that make them lie.

entry.title: Stir the Pot First: Population, Sample, and Why We Guess
entry.summary: Why a sip judges a pot of tea only if you stir it: population versus sample, four ways to draw a sample, the poll that asked 2.4 million and still erred.

entry.title: The Number on the Tin: Mean, Median and Mode
entry.summary: Why a perfectly computed average can describe nobody: "typical" is ambiguous, and mean, median and mode are three honest answers to three different questions. Look at the picture first.

entry.title: Ansible Cheatsheet: Every Step from the Series
entry.summary: The Ansible series as direct steps - pinned install, ansible.cfg, inventory and host keys, ad-hoc commands, idempotent playbooks with handlers, a role, rolling maintenance, vault.

entry.title: The Laptop That Ran Ansible 2.16: An Install You Can Trust
entry.summary: A pinned Ansible install per project, which Python the control machine and the nodes need, ansible.cfg, SSH host keys, and the errors you hit on the first runs.

entry.title: The Playbook That Restarted slurmd Every Night: Idempotence and Handlers
entry.summary: Why a playbook should report changed only when it changed something, templates instead of shell, handlers that restart only when needed, --check --diff, and the handler that never ran.

entry.title: Four Nodes Said "Too Many Open Files": Inventories and Ad-Hoc Commands
entry.summary: Inventory groups and ranges, groupvars with overrides, targeting patterns, ad-hoc commands across the cluster, the node that was down, and checking a change in a fresh login.

entry.title: The GPU Node That Thought It Had 1000 MB: Roles and Variables
entry.summary: Turn a playbook into a role, load OS-specific variables with firstfound, put site values in defaults not vars, use hostvars for per-node values in templates, and check every node got the same config.

entry.title: The Reboot That Killed a Week of Jobs: Rolling Maintenance with Slurm
entry.summary: Change busy compute nodes safely - drain through Slurm, wait for jobs, one canary first, stop on the first failure, check the node really came back, a dry run that is really dry, and rollback.
